title: What does belonging mean?
essentialQuestion: What helps people feel part of a community?
learningGoal: Explain how a group can change the way it works so that more people feel they belong, without anyone having to share private information.

warmUp.question: Which of these can be a group where people feel they belong?

evidence.label: Fictional example created for this lesson.
evidence.question: What does each card tell you about what makes the club easy or hard to join?

cases.name: Card 1
cases.body: “I joined after someone explained the rules to me quietly, one to one.”

cases.name: Card 2
cases.body: “Meetings are hard for me when everyone speaks at once.”

cases.name: Card 3
cases.body: “I want to help choose the activities, not only attend them.”

cards.title: Changes the club is thinking about
items: A welcome partner for each new member
A student planning group that helps choose activities

sections.heading: Belonging is more than being there
sections.text: Belonging is the feeling of being accepted and connected to a group. A person can sit in a room with a group and still feel ignored or left out. People can belong to many kinds of groups at once, such as a class, a sports team, a group of friends or a club. It might also be people who share a language or a hobby. Many cultures value these connections. In southern Africa, people often talk about Ubuntu. It is usually explained as “a person is a person through other people”. It means we grow as people through our relationships with others.
sections.simpler: Belonging means you feel accepted in a group. You feel connected to the people in it. A person can be in a room and still feel left out. People can belong to many groups. It can be a class, a team or friends. It can be people who share a language or a hobby. In southern Africa, people talk about Ubuntu. It means we grow as people through other people.

sections.heading: Groups can remove barriers
sections.text: A barrier is something that makes it harder for someone to take part. Look at the youth club's feedback cards. One member finds meetings difficult when everyone speaks at once. Another member only joined after someone explained the rules quietly. The club does not need to change its members. Instead, it can change how it works. Turn-taking rules make meetings easier to follow, because only one person speaks at a time. A welcome partner can explain the club's routines to new members. These changes remove barriers, so more people can participate.
sections.simpler: A barrier makes it hard to take part. Read the club's cards. One person finds it hard when everyone talks at once. One person joined after someone explained the rules. The club does not need to change its members. It can change how it works. With turn-taking, one person speaks at a time. A welcome partner can explain the routines. Now more people can join in.

sections.heading: Everyone can have a say
sections.text: Belonging also grows when people have a real say. One card says: “I want to help choose the activities, not only attend them”. A student planning group gives members more agency, which means the power to make choices and act. The UN agreement on children's rights says children have the right to give their opinions on things that affect them. It also says they can join or set up groups. A good group asks members what is working and what is not. Nobody should have to share private things about their life to belong.
sections.simpler: Belonging grows when people have a say. One member wants to help choose what the club does. A planning group gives members more agency. They can make choices and act. A UN agreement says children have a right to give their opinions. They can join groups or start them. A good group asks what works and what does not. No one has to share private things to belong.

checks.question: Which change could help the member who finds meetings hard?

options.text: A bigger room for club meetings
options.feedback: Not quite. The problem is that everyone speaks at once, not the size of the room. Look at card 2.
Not quite. Louder voices would not help if everyone still speaks at once. Look at card 2.
Yes. This member finds it hard when everyone speaks at once. With turn-taking, one person speaks at a time.

checks.question: Which change gives members more agency?

options.feedback: Yes. A planning group lets members help choose activities, so they have a real say.

options.text: A longer list of club rules
options.feedback: Not quite. More rules do not give members a say. Look for a change that lets members make choices.
Not quite. If only adults lead, members have less say. Look for a change that lets members make choices.

checks.question: How could the club find out if its changes are helping?
checks.placeholder: Think about simple ways to ask members, such as a question box or a quick vote ...

write.prompt: Suggest two changes for the youth club. For each one, name the card it answers and say why it may help.
sentenceStarters: This answers the card that says ...
The club could check if it works by ...
selfCheck: I linked each change to a feedback card.
I changed how the club works, not the members.
write.example: I recommend turn-taking rules in meetings. This answers the card that says meetings are hard when everyone speaks at once. It may help because only one person speaks at a time. I also recommend a student planning group. This answers the member who wants to help choose activities. It may help because members get a real say. The club could check if it works by asking members what they think after a month.

speak.partnerTask: Practise inviting a quiet member into a pretend planning meeting. Ask kindly, and make it easy for them to say no.
speak.independentTask: Explain one way a class, team or club can help more people feel they belong.

watch.title: Youth Voices: Locating Identity, Agency, & Belonging in all Learning Spaces
watch.why: Young people share their own views on identity, agency and belonging in the places where they learn.
watch.beforeQuestion: What is the difference between being invited to a group and having a real say in it?
watch.afterQuestion: What is one thing adults or other young people can do to help someone have a real say?
watch.summary: In this video, young people talk about identity, belonging and agency in the places where they learn. Their identity grows from their experiences. These include goals they reached and mistakes they learned from. Belonging grows when adults know students' names. It also grows when students can share their work and not be judged. For them, agency means feeling sure that you can reach a goal if you work at it. Older helpers, friends and chances to lead can help. At the end, they tell adults that young people are ready to help shape their own lives and schools. The speakers share their own stories, but you do not need to share yours. You can think about the questions using the youth club, or a group you know.
keyPoints: Belonging grows when people know your name and you can share without being judged.
Agency means feeling sure you can reach a goal, with help from others.
Young people are ready to help shape their own schools and lives.
watch.contentNote: Contains personal reflections from young people about their identity. No learner needs to share personal experiences. Preview it first, and let learners use the written summary instead if they prefer.

visual.description: A youth club meeting in a circle of chairs. One young person is speaking while holding a small “talking stone”, and the others are listening. At the side, a welcome partner sits next to a new member and points to a simple poster of club rules with pictures. On the wall, a planning board has sticky notes with activity ideas: football, drawing, music and cooking.
visual.alt: Young people sit in a circle while one person speaks and the others listen. A new member sits with a welcome partner, and a board on the wall shows ideas for activities.

educatorNotes: Please have a local educator review this lesson before use. Belonging can bring up feelings about home, family or loss for some learners.
Never ask learners to talk about their own home, family, past or times they did not belong. The youth club, a class, a team, a group of friends, a language or a hobby always work as examples.
If a learner chooses to share something personal, listen calmly, thank them, and do not ask follow-up questions in front of the group. Follow your centre's safeguarding steps if you are worried.
The video shows young people reflecting on their identity. Preview it first; the written summary can be used instead.
